analysis.one_liner: Nullifies the new overtime rule that would have extended overtime pay to millions of salaried workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with 45 Republican cosponsors, it sat in committee through one related hearing and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2015 the Department of Labor proposed raising the salary cutoff under which salaried workers must be paid overtime, a jump the bill's own text puts at 113 percent in its first year [S3]. This bill would erase that rule by statute, void it retroactively if already final, and bar the Department from issuing anything similar without years of new economic analysis, a minimum one-year waiting period, and a fresh rulemaking for every future change to the threshold [S3]. It would also prohibit any automatic annual updates to the threshold, meaning the cutoff would stay fixed until Congress or a future rulemaking moved it [S2]. The bill never reached the Senate floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers with substantial numbers of salaried workers earning between the old threshold and the new one — retail and restaurant chains, banks, nonprofits, universities, health care providers, and small businesses — would avoid having to either raise those salaries to the new cutoff or start paying them overtime. The bill's findings section is built on compliance-cost objections from business commenters and the Small Business Administration's advocacy office [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers of salaried workers near the threshold

how_it_helps.text: Wipes out the Department of Labor rule that raised the overtime salary threshold — a 113 percent increase in its first year, according to the bill's own findings [S3].
If the rule were already final when the bill passed, the Department could not enforce it for past conduct and workers would lose any right to sue over pre-enactment noncompliance [S3].

Blocks any substantially similar rule unless the Department completes a long list of new studies covering small entities, regions, nonprofits, health care providers, and school districts, then waits at least a year after publication before the rule takes effect [S3].
Prohibits automatic annual updates to the salary threshold and requires a brand-new notice-and-comment rulemaking for every future change [S2].
Bars the Department from changing the duties tests (the rules deciding who counts as an exempt manager or professional) beyond what was specifically proposed for public comment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Salaried workers earning between the old cutoff and the new one would keep working long hours without overtime pay, with no protection from erosion of the threshold over time.
analysis.who_pays_short: Salaried workers earning under the new cutoff

drawbacks.text: The bill's findings acknowledge the threshold increase was steep, and cite the Small Business Administration's advocacy office arguing the Department's analysis of small entities and regional cost-of-living differences was inadequate [S3].

Business commenters argued reclassified workers could lose workplace flexibility arrangements, and multi-state employers faced reclassification complications across regions with different pay scales — the strongest good-faith case for a more gradual or regionally adjusted approach [S3].

By banning automatic updates, the bill would freeze the salary threshold so it loses value to inflation every year until someone runs a full new rulemaking — a design that guarantees the cutoff becomes outdated [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have spared some employers compliance costs and answered real procedural complaints about the rule's economic analysis. But its core effect was to permanently deny overtime protections to a large group of salaried workers, and its ban on automatic updates would quietly erode the threshold over time. The procedural concerns it raised could have been addressed through a narrower, revised rule rather than nullification and a wall of new preconditions.

outcome.mechanism: It never came to a vote: introduced in March 2016 and referred to the Senate health and labor committee, which took no further action beyond a related Small Business Committee hearing, and the 114th Congress ended with the bill still in committee [S5].

narrative.text: Tim Scott introduced the bill on March 17, 2016, joined by Lamar Alexander, and it was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S5].
All 45 of its cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on [S4].
The only further action in the record was a May 11, 2016 hearing by the Senate Small Business and Entrepreneurship Committee [S5].
The bill was never reported out of committee, never scheduled for a floor vote, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].
The rule it targeted, described in the CRS summary, would have raised the salary threshold under which salaried workers must receive overtime and prevented automatic annual updates to it [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who opposed the higher overtime threshold came out ahead overall. This bill died without a vote, and the rule it targeted never took effect as written either — a federal court blocked it in late 2016 before its compliance date, and it was later rewritten with a far smaller increase, so workers between the old and new cutoffs never saw the raise either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who opposed the overtime expansion

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 45 cosponsors was a Republican, and no Democrat signed on [S4].

industries.industry: Retail, restaurant, and other employers of salaried workers below the new threshold
industries.note: These employers would have had to either raise salaries to the new cutoff or start paying overtime to millions of workers. Killing the rule keeps that cost off their books and keeps long hours unpaid for the workers affected [S3].

industries.industry: Nonprofit organizations and Medicare/Medicaid-dependent health care providers
industries.note: The bill singles these employers out for special cost analysis before any similar rule, reflecting their complaints about reclassifying staff. Avoiding the threshold saves them money but leaves their low-paid salaried staff working without overtime [S3].
The Small Business Administration's advocacy office argued the rule's impact on small entities was underestimated; the bill would have removed the compliance burden entirely [S3].

industries.industry: Department of Labor rulemaking authority over overtime exemptions
industries.note: The bill voids the rule and hobbles any future attempt: exhaustive new studies, a one-year minimum delay, no automatic updates, and a fresh rulemaking for every threshold change. This narrows the executive branch's ability to update wage standards without Congress [S3].
